newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Conservatives boosted by debates - poll.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Conservatives boosted by debates - poll.

text.p: Canada's once-mighty Conservatives, struggling to recover from near annihilation in the 1993 federal election, got a bounce from this week's televised campaign debates, a Reuters poll showed on Friday.

In the first survey released since the debates, voters declared Conservative leader Jean Charest the winner, helping his party cut the lead of Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberals by six points in the runup to the June 2 election.
The Liberals still led the Conservatives, their nearest rivals in the election race, by 25 points, according to the poll conducted for Reuters on May 14 and 15 by Zogby International.
The poll showed Charest gathering momentum, especially in the Atlantic provinces. But as the numbers stand now, the Liberals lead in all regions and would win re-election.
Almost three voters in 10, however, said they had not made up their minds.
"Despite a very strong performance by Charest in both debates, it clearly doesn't appear it was enough to shake the broad and deep support for the Liberals," said John Zogby, who conducted the poll.
"But Charest is going a long way to rehabilitate the Tories (Conservatives) and is clearly a potential prime minister of the future, especially if the jobs issue hurts Chretien's second term."

The poll showed the Liberals leading the race with 45.4 percent of the decided vote, to 20.4 percent for the Conservatives, 15.8 percent for Reform, 9.9 percent for the New Democratic Party and 7.5 percent for the separatist Bloc Quebecois.
The last Reuters-Zogby poll, taken May 1 to 4, gave the Liberals a 31-point lead over the Conservatives.
After nine years in power, the Tories were devastated in the last election, collapsing to two members, one of them Charest, in the 295-seat House of Commons.
The stunning rebuke came in response to the Conservative government's perceived corruption and failure to solve economic and social ills.

The youthful Charest has crisscrossed Canada seeking to rebuild support, but had been unable to build regional power bases, crucial since members of Parliament are elected on the basis of the most votes in each electoral district.

By a three-to-one margin, however, Charest was declared the winner of nationally televised debates on Monday and Tuesday -- 43.7 percent said he won, versus 13.5 percent for Chretien and 7.8 percent for Preston Manning of the right-wing Reform Party.
The new poll showed that for the first time, Charest was in a virtual tie with Chretien in one of Canada's regions, the Atlantic provinces, which have 32 of the new Parliament's 301 seats.

"I think what Charest has done is made the Conservatives a real player for second place," said Zogby, whose firm Zogby International was the only polling group to call the U.S. presidential election correctly last year.

But he pointed out that Reform is "mighty from the Prairies west." Because its strength is more concentrated -- giving it leading support in more districts -- analysts have suggested it might form the official opposition even if it trails the Conservatives nationally.

Chretien maintained a virtually unassailable lead in the big electoral prize, Ontario, with 55 percent support to Charest's 18 percent and Manning's 17 percent. Reform and Conservative split the right-wing vote in Ontario last election, giving the Liberals all but one seat. The Liberals looked set for another near sweep.
In French-speaking Quebec, the Liberals had a 12-point lead over the Bloc Quebecois and 18 points over the Conservatives.
In all provincial or regional breakdowns, the margin of error is substantially higher than the 3.2 points for the national poll, which covered 1,009 likely voters.

Among Quebec voters, the poll showed only 35 percent favored sovereignty compared with 58 percent against. The poll question was similar to that posed in the province's 1995 referendum -- whether Quebec should become sovereign after having made a formal offer to Canada for a new partnership.

Chretien's main economic legacy in his 3-1/2-year term has been to slash Canada's chronic fiscal deficits. The deficit cutting has prompted sharply lower interest rates, but left unemployment stubbornly high, above nine percent.

Reform and the Conservatives argue that tax cuts will create jobs, while the left-wing New Democrats have pushed for more spending. National unity and social issues such as gun control have also figured in voter intentions.

Fifty-two percent of those polled said they felt Canada was headed in the right direction, while 32 percent -- including pluralities in the Prairie and Atlantic provinces -- said things were on the wrong track.
